critical.title: Exported ContentProvider exposes an injectable SQL query
critical.description:
Two findings in this app combine into a single exploitable path: "Exported provider NotesProvider has no permission protection" and "SQL injection in NotesProvider query() method".

Attack path:
1. Attacker app crafts a malicious URI
2. Attacker app calls getContentResolver().query() on jakhar.aseem.diva.NotesProvider
3. NotesProvider.query() receives the malicious URI
4. The URI segment is concatenated into the SQL WHERE clause
5. The SQLite database executes the injected SQL query
critical.impact: Any installed app can query the provider, and the query is built by string concatenation, so the caller controls the SQL. The whole database is readable - and writable where the provider allows it - by an app that declares no permissions at all.
critical.recommendation: Set android:exported="false" if no other app needs the provider. If it does, use parameterised selection arguments only, and validate the projection and sort order against a fixed allowlist.

medium.title: Backup-enabled app stores credentials in local storage
medium.description:
5 findings in this app combine into one exploitable path: "Application data is backup-enabled", "Credential stored in SharedPreferences in plain text (putString)", "Credential stored in a SQLite database in plain text (execSQL)", "Credential written to a temporary file (createTempFile)" and "User PIN stored in plaintext in SharedPreferences".

Attack path:
1. Attacker connects device via USB
2. Attacker executes adb backup
3. Android backs up the app's internal data directory
4. Attacker extracts the backup file
5. Attacker reads the plaintext credentials from the SharedPreferences XML file used by InsecureDataStorage1Activity
medium.impact: Backup copies the app's private storage, and that storage holds a credential. For an app targeting below Android 12 (API 31), or a debuggable one, `adb backup` does it over USB without root, so anyone with a minute at an unlocked phone walks away with the credential; for newer targets it travels in cloud and device-transfer backups.
medium.recommendation: Set android:allowBackup="false", or exclude the credential store via android:dataExtractionRules. Keep tokens in EncryptedSharedPreferences or the Keystore rather than plain SharedPreferences.

info.description: android:allowBackup is "true", so `adb backup` copies the app's private data off the device over USB, without root. The application allows backups (android:allowBackup="true"), which can lead to sensitive data stored in the internal app directory (such as the divanotes.db database used by NotesProvider) being extracted via adb backup.
info.impact: Any locally stored credentials or PII become extractable over USB.
info.recommendation: Set android:allowBackup="false", or exclude sensitive files with android:dataExtractionRules (android:fullBackupContent below Android 12).

reasons: Backup-extractable app data. Backup is a documented platform feature and on by default. What matters is what would be in the backup: name a credential in app storage and this becomes a real extraction path.
Confirmed as part of chain-002: Backup-enabled app stores credentials in local storage.

info.title: Application is debuggable in this build
info.description: android:debuggable="true" lets any user with adb attach a debugger to the process, read and modify memory, and inspect application data. The application is marked as debuggable in the manifest (android:debuggable="true"), which allows an attacker with ADB access to attach a debugger and inspect the application's memory and state.
info.impact: Full runtime access to the app's process and data on any device with adb.
info.recommendation: Remove android:debuggable or set it to "false" for release builds.

reasons: Debuggable release build. A debuggable build is a release-pipeline defect rather than an exploitable flaw - attaching a debugger already requires ADB access to the device. Worth fixing, not worth a severity.

info.title: No network security config declared
info.description: The app declares neither android:networkSecurityConfig nor usesCleartextTraffic, so it relies on platform defaults and pins no domain. With targetSdkVersion 23 those defaults still permit cleartext HTTP (see the cleartext finding).
info.impact: Without pinning, anyone who gets a CA trusted on the device can read and alter the app's TLS traffic.
info.recommendation: Declare a network security config that disables cleartext and pins the domains that carry sensitive traffic.

reasons: No certificate pinning. Pinning defends against an attacker who already controls a trusted CA or the device's trust store. Without one of those, TLS is still doing its job. It becomes a finding when paired with what the unpinned channel actually carries.

info.title: No screenshot protection: FLAG_SECURE is never set
info.description: Nothing in the app sets WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_SECURE, so every screen can be screenshotted or recorded and appears in the recent-apps snapshot.
info.impact: Credentials, balances or personal data on screen end up in screenshots, screen recordings and the task-switcher preview.
info.recommendation: Set FLAG_SECURE on the windows of screens that show credentials or account data.

reasons: Screen contents not protected from capture. Without FLAG_SECURE, what a screen shows can end up in screenshots, screen recordings and the task-switcher preview. That matters on screens showing credentials, card numbers or balances; on its own it is a hardening note.

info.title: targetSdkVersion 23 allows implicit component export
info.description: On targetSdk 23, any component with an intent-filter is exported unless it says otherwise.
info.recommendation: Raise targetSdkVersion to 31+ and declare android:exported explicitly on every filtered component.

reasons: Legacy platform behaviour from SDK levels. An SDK level is a statement about which platform defaults apply, not a defect. It is context for the findings that depend on those defaults - pair it with one of them.
warnings: Implicit export only applies below targetSdk 31; confirm the app's targetSdkVersion before treating this as exploitable.

info.title: targetSdkVersion 23 trusts user-installed CA certificates
info.description: Below API 24 the app trusts the user CA store, so a user-installed certificate can intercept HTTPS. The attacker first has to get a CA installed on the victim's device, which is why this is not graded as a trust-all TLS bypass.

reasons: User-installed CA certificates trusted. Trusting the user CA store lets someone who first gets a CA onto the device intercept HTTPS; it is not a trust-all bypass. Name the sensitive traffic on that channel and this becomes a real interception path.

info.title: Task hijacking (StrandHogg) possible on Android 10 and lower
info.description: minSdkVersion 15 lets the app run on Android versions before 11, and its task affinity is its package name "jakhar.aseem.diva". There, another app can declare the same affinity, with allowTaskReparenting, and have its own activity shown in this app's task.
info.impact: On a device running Android 10 or lower, a malicious app can put a look-alike screen on top of this app's task, phishing credentials or keeping the real app from being shown.
info.recommendation: Raise minSdkVersion to 30, where Android fixed this. Until then, android:taskAffinity="" on the <application> mitigates the original attack, though not its runtime variant on unpatched Android 9 and lower.
